standard.question: What did you change?
standard.answer: ranker_model: lambdamart_v6 -> lambdamart_v7; nothing else differs between arms

standard.question: Is the data trustworthy?
standard.answer: Yes, as far as the checks reach; not checked: pre period

standard.question: Is the effect real, or chance?
standard.answer: Successful Search Rate +0.00% (-0.30% to +0.30%); its interval includes zero. Across the scorecard 4 of 57 metrics moved clearly; about 2.9 would by chance alone

standard.question: Will it last?
standard.answer: Probably: effect by days since exposure: first days -0.01%, last days +0.01% (trend +0.002% per day)

standard.question: Did the change do what it was built to do?
standard.answer: Not shown. If the scorecard or a cut has a coverage metric (the share of queries whose top results changed), register it as feature_metrics

standard.question: Metric families used:
standard.answer: abandonment = Abandonment Rate, ad_ctr = Ad Click Rate, autocomplete = Autocomplete Acceptance, clicks_per_user = Clicks per User, ctr = CTR, latency = Latency p95 (ms), long_click = Long Click Rate, pagination = Pagination Rate, queries_per_user = Queries per User, reformulation = Reformulation Rate, revenue = Revenue per User, sessions_per_user = Sessions per User, success = Successful Search Rate, time_to_click = Time to First Click (s), zero_result = Zero Result Rate

questions.question: Successful Search Rate was expected to rise but didn't move. Why?

patterns.name: Slower results cost engagement
patterns.label: inferred
patterns.mechanism: The treatment serves results more slowly, and slower pages lose clicks and raise abandonment, which can hide a relevance gain. Speed effects tend to grow over weeks rather than fade.
patterns.source: Brutlag, Google, 2009 (400 ms delay: -0.44% searches in weeks 1-3, -0.76% in weeks 4-6, still -0.21% after removal); Dmitriev et al., A Dirty Dozen: Twelve Common Metric Interpretation Pitfalls, KDD 2017 (latency moved by page mix)
evidence: Successful Search Rate didn't move clearly (+0.00% (-0.30% to +0.30%))

deep_dives.cut: abandonment and CTR by latency bucket, per arm
deep_dives.confirms: the loss sits in the slow buckets
deep_dives.refutes: the loss is flat across latency buckets

deep_dives.cut: latency by page type and load type (cached reloads vs fresh loads), by arm
deep_dives.confirms: latency rises on the same page types
deep_dives.refutes: the page mix changed, so latency moved without pages getting slower

deep_dives.cut: effect by device and network type
deep_dives.confirms: mobile or slow networks carry the loss
deep_dives.refutes: the loss is the same everywhere

deep_dives.cut: relevance metrics on queries where latency didn't change
deep_dives.confirms: relevance improves once latency is held fixed
deep_dives.refutes: no gain even at equal latency

patterns.name: Worse results make users give up
patterns.label: inferred
patterns.mechanism: Users leave without clicking because results got worse, not because the answer was on the page.
patterns.source: Li, Huffman, Tokuda, SIGIR 2009 (good vs bad abandonment); Song, Shi, Fu, WWW 2013
evidence: Successful Search Rate didn't move clearly (+0.00% (-0.30% to +0.30%))

deep_dives.cut: abandonment on queries with an answer or rich snippet vs without
deep_dives.confirms: the rise sits on queries without an answer
deep_dives.refutes: the rise sits on answer-bearing queries

deep_dives.cut: config diff of presentation parameters (answers, rich snippets)
deep_dives.refutes: an answer or snippet parameter differs

ruled_out.name: Answers on the page reduce clicks
ruled_out.label: inferred
ruled_out.mechanism: More users get their answer from the results page itself (answers, richer snippets), so they leave without clicking and don't retry.
ruled_out.source: Li, Huffman, Tokuda, SIGIR 2009 (good abandonment, higher on mobile); Pew Research 2025 (clicks 8% vs 15% with AI summaries)
evidence: Successful Search Rate didn't move clearly (+0.00% (-0.30% to +0.30%))

deep_dives.cut: abandonment on queries with an answer or rich snippet vs without
deep_dives.confirms: the rise sits on answer-bearing queries
deep_dives.refutes: the rise sits on queries without an answer

deep_dives.cut: a similar query issued again within 5 minutes after an abandoned query
deep_dives.confirms: abandoned users don't come back to retry

deep_dives.cut: config diff of presentation parameters (answers, rich snippets)
deep_dives.confirms: an answer or snippet parameter differs between arms
deep_dives.refutes: only ranking differs (this doesn't rule it out: ranking can surface such results too)

deep_dives.confirms: the rise is larger on mobile, where good abandonment is common
deep_dives.refutes: the rise is the same on desktop

ruled_out.name: Some queries win, others lose
ruled_out.label: inferred
ruled_out.mechanism: The change helps many queries and hurts others, so averages hide both: more clicks overall while a slice of queries is abandoned more.
ruled_out.source: Dmitriev et al., A Dirty Dozen: Twelve Common Metric Interpretation Pitfalls, KDD 2017 (heterogeneous effects); reasoned from averages hiding opposite effects
evidence: Successful Search Rate didn't move clearly (+0.00% (-0.30% to +0.30%))
